summary: Defines how Opus-encoded speech and audio is packaged into RTP packets, including an applicability statement and media type registrations. It lets the Opus codec be used in real-time applications.

eli5.summary: How to pack pieces of a sound recording into small parcels so they can be shipped quickly and put back together.

questions: how to send opus over rtp
what is the opus rtp payload format
what is the audio/opus media type
what rtp clock rate does opus use
subtitle: How Opus-encoded speech and music is carried in RTP packets, and how to describe it in SDP.

tldr.problem: The Opus codec produces compressed speech and audio, but real-time applications need a standard way to put those frames into RTP packets and to tell the other side how to use them.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload carries exactly one Opus packet, the RTP timestamp always runs on a 48000 Hz clock, and a registered audio/opus media type with optional parameters is mapped into SDP.
tldr.outcome: Opus can be used in real-time applications such as conferencing and Voice over IP with consistent packetization and negotiation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7587 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The Opus codec it carries is defined in RFC 6716.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Opus is a speech and audio codec developed in the IETF. The RFC describes it as having a very low algorithmic delay and being highly scalable in audio bandwidth, bitrate and complexity, with different modes for speech and for music.

This document defines the RTP payload format for Opus: how encoded audio is packetized for the Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550). It also gives an applicability statement for using Opus over RTP and registers the media type for the payload format. The codec itself is defined in RFC 6716.
sections.eli5: Opus is a clever way to shrink sound. This RFC explains how to pack that shrunk sound into network parcels.

sections.title: What the Opus Codec Offers
sections.content:
Opus has a voice mode and an audio mode. The voice mode encodes speech efficiently at lower bitrates, while the audio mode is tuned for general audio at medium and higher bitrates. Bitrates run from 6 kbit/s to 510 kbit/s and can change at any moment.

For a 20 ms frame size, the RFC lists bitrate sweet spots: 8-12 kbit/s for narrowband speech, 16-20 kbit/s for wideband speech, 28-40 kbit/s for fullband speech, 48-64 kbit/s for fullband mono music and 64-128 kbit/s for fullband stereo music. The average bitrate SHOULD NOT exceed the available network bandwidth.

Variable bitrate (VBR) gives better quality than constant bitrate for the same average, and is the best choice for most voice. Constant bitrate may be chosen to avoid a possible information leak when encrypting. In that case the Opus padding mechanism is the RECOMMENDED way to pad, because the RTP padding bit is unencrypted.

Discontinuous transmission (DTX) skips sending silence. A receiver can tell DTX from packet loss by gaps in the sequence number, and the decoder fills the gap with comfort noise. Using the separate Comfort Noise payload of RFC 3389 is discouraged. A sender MUST drop whole frames only, so successive timestamps differ by a multiple of 120. Because DTX lowers quality slightly, continuous transmission is RECOMMENDED unless bandwidth is severely limited.

The voice mode can embed in-band forward error correction (FEC): packet N carries redundant data about packet N-1. The encoder alone decides whether to include it, so the payload needs no special handling. If the receiver cannot use FEC, FEC SHOULD NOT be used. Stereo is signaled inside the Opus bitstream, and if a decoder cannot benefit from stereo, the sender SHOULD NOT send it.
sections.eli5: Opus has a voice setting and a music setting, and it can turn the sound quality up or down like a dial. It can also skip sending silence and add a little backup information in case a parcel gets lost.

sections.title: The RTP Payload Format
sections.content:
An Opus RTP packet is just the RTP header followed by the Opus payload. The RTP header is used as in RFC 3550; the timestamp, sequence number and marker bit follow Section 4.1 of RFC 3551. The payload type is assigned dynamically. Opus payloads are whole octets, so padding is not needed, although the Opus internal padding is preferred if padding is used.

An encoder can output frames of 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 40 or 60 ms. Any number of frames can be combined into a packet, up to a maximum packet duration of 120 ms. An RTP payload MUST contain exactly one Opus packet as defined in Section 3 of RFC 6716.

The RTP timestamp always runs at 48000 Hz for every Opus mode and sampling rate, counting samples per single mono channel. For input at other sampling rates, the rate is adjusted to 48000 Hz. Each frame advances the timestamp by a fixed amount, and a packet with several frames advances it by the sum. Receivers MUST be ready for duplicate RTP packets, MUST pass at most one copy to the decoder, and MUST discard the others.
sections.eli5: Each parcel holds one bundle of sound, up to a tenth of a second and a bit. The clock on every parcel counts the same way no matter how the sound was recorded, so the listener can put the parcels in order.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
Opus helps with congestion because its target bitrate can be changed at any time. The amount of audio in each packet can also be used: the transmission rate is inversely proportional to the packet duration. Fewer, longer packets cut header overhead but increase latency and loss sensitivity, so this ought to be used with care.

UDP provides no congestion control, so applications that use RTP over UDP SHOULD implement their own above the UDP layer, as described in RFC 5405. The RFC points to work in the RMCAT working group on how the RTP layer, codec control layer and transport interface interact.
sections.eli5: If the road is jammed, the sender can make the parcels smaller or send them less often. That helps traffic move, though waiting longer to fill a bigger parcel makes the sound arrive later.

sections.title: The audio/opus Media Type
sections.content:
The IANA section registers one media subtype, audio/opus. Its one required parameter is rate, which is always the 48000 Hz timestamp clock. The rest are optional hints and preferences:

  • maxplaybackrate and sprop-maxcapturerate: the highest sampling rate the receiver can play, and the highest the sender is likely to produce. Values run from 8000 to 48000, and both default to 48000.
  • ptime and maxptime: the preferred and maximum packet duration in milliseconds. Defaults are 20 and 120, up to a maximum of 120.
  • maxaveragebitrate: the maximum average receive bitrate in bit/s. Values outside 6000 to 510000 SHOULD be ignored.
  • stereo and sprop-stereo: whether the receiver prefers stereo, and whether the sender is likely to send it. Both default to 0 (mono). Every receiver MUST still be able to decode stereo.
  • cbr: 1 for constant bitrate, 0 (the default) for variable.
  • useinbandfec and usedtx: whether the decoder can use in-band FEC, and whether it prefers DTX. Both default to 0.

For transfer over RTP, the payload format of Section 4 SHALL be used.
sections.eli5: These are like the settings on a form you fill in before a phone call: how good your speakers are, whether you want stereo, how big the parcels should be. Anything you leave blank gets a sensible default.

sections.title: SDP Mapping and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
In the Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566), the media type audio goes in the m= line and opus in a=rtpmap. The clock rate there MUST be 48000 and the number of channels MUST be 2, whatever the actual audio. The parameters ptime and maxptime map to their own attributes, and most of the others go in a=fmtp as semicolon-separated name=value pairs. The two sprop- parameters may also appear in a source-level attribute, which overrides the a=fmtp line.

For the offer/answer exchange of RFC 3264, the parameters ptime, maxptime, maxplaybackrate, maxaveragebitrate, stereo, cbr, useinbandfec and usedtx are one-direction, receive-only settings. A sender MUST NOT exceed the receiver's maxaveragebitrate, and MUST NOT use stereo to a single destination when stereo is 0. The sprop- parameters describe the sender and do not affect interoperability. Unknown parameters in an offer MUST be ignored and removed from the answer.

For declarative use of SDP, such as the Session Announcement Protocol or RTSP, ptime, maxptime and the like are recommendations by the decoding side, while the other parameters are declarative and a participant MUST use them.
sections.eli5: Before the call, each side writes its wishes on a card and swaps cards. Some cards say what I would like to hear, and some say what I will probably send. If one side sees a wish it does not understand, it just ignores it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using VBR is subject to the considerations in RFC 6562. Opus RTP packets are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and of any RTP profile in use, such as the secure profile built on SRTP (RFC 3711).

As RFC 7202 explains, an RTP payload format is not responsible for mandating how confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity are provided. That falls on whoever uses RTP in an application, who can find guidance in RFC 7201. Applications SHOULD use one or more appropriate strong security mechanisms.

The payload format and Opus encoding show no significant non-uniformity in receiver computational load, so they are unlikely to give a denial-of-service threat through pathological datagrams.
sections.eli5: This RFC does not lock the parcels itself. If the sound is private, the app has to use a secure way of sending it, and the RFC says it should.
